title: The Cash Filed Under Boring

beats.text: In nineteen twenty-six, a stock sold for sixty-five dollars with ninety-five in cash inside.
Imagine you're Benjamin Graham, reading dull pipeline reports in Washington.
Wall Street never opens these. Too boring.
Then you spot Northern Pipe Line, a Standard Oil spin-off.
Its pipes earn peanuts. Its drawer is stuffed with railroad bonds.
So why would anyone sell money at a discount?
You buy shares and visit the bosses.
Pipelines are complex, they say. Don't like it? Sell your shares.
At the meeting in Oil City, nobody even seconds your motion.
You collect proxies, and by nineteen twenty-eight you win two board seats.
You see, it's a yard-sale wallet: sixty-five dollars, ninety-five inside. Nobody opens it.
The market priced the sleepy pipes, not the drawer.
Suddenly the company agrees to pay out seventy dollars a share.
The money was never hidden. It was just filed under boring.

facts.claim: In 1926 Benjamin Graham found the pipeline data in Interstate Commerce Commission annual reports and studied the full filings in Washington (ICC reading room)
Northern Pipe Line was one of the pipeline companies spun off from Standard Oil in 1911
The stock sold at $65 while holding about $95 per share of cash assets, mostly high-grade railroad bonds; its operating revenue was small (about $300,000 vs $3.6m of bonds)
Graham bought about 5% of the shares (2,000 of 40,000) and met management, who said the pipeline business was complex/specialised and that if he did not approve he should sell his shares
At the annual meeting in Oil City, Pennsylvania, nobody seconded Graham's motion and the meeting adjourned
At the 1928 annual meeting Graham held proxies for about 38% of the shares and his side won two board seats
The company then agreed to distribute $70 per share to shareholders ($50 at once plus $20 promised, per Gurufocus)
The information came from public filings that Wall Street had not bothered to read (yard-sale wallet is the narrator's analogy, not a historical claim)

caption:
1926: a stock trades at $65 with $95 a share of bonds inside. Everyone could see it. Nobody read it.
Benjamin Graham did, and went to war with the board in Oil City.
